listening.title: Booking a short residential course
listening.script:
Administrator: Oak House adult learning centre. How may I help?
Caller: I’d like information about the weekend course on making radio programmes. I’ve listened to the sample online and it sounds practical, but I need to check accommodation and travel before booking. I’ll be coming from another town.
Administrator: Certainly. The course includes a room on Friday and Saturday nights, though meals have separate arrangements. Could I take your surname in case we need to continue the booking later?
Caller: It’s Varden, V-A-R-D-E-N. I’ve never stayed at the centre. Is the building close to public transport, or would I need to hire a car?
Administrator: You won’t need a car. Come to Brook station, not the larger station at Hillgate. People sometimes choose Hillgate because more trains stop there, but the onward connection is much less convenient. From Brook there’s a local bus that stops at our gate.
Caller: I can get there on Friday evening. What time can I collect the room key? The train I’d prefer arrives at about five.
Administrator: Reception opens for arriving residents at four thirty, so 4:30 is the earliest. Before then the rooms are being checked. If your train is later, someone will be here until eight. Please tell us if you expect to arrive after that rather than assuming the front door will stay open.
Caller: Fine. What is the full course fee? I saw two prices on an old leaflet.
Administrator: The residential weekend is one hundred and sixty-eight pounds. The lower figure, one hundred and twenty, is for people who attend teaching sessions but sleep elsewhere. It isn’t a discount available just because you’re travelling by train. Your booking would be £168 before optional meals.
Caller: And how much do I pay to secure a place?
Administrator: A deposit of forty pounds. The rest is due two weeks before the course. We can hold a provisional place until tomorrow while you check the trains, but it isn’t confirmed until we receive the deposit.
---
Caller: Are the rooms shared? I’m happy working with other people all day, but I’d prefer somewhere quiet in the evening.
Administrator: Most are single rooms. There are a few twins for friends booking together, but we never assign a stranger to share without agreement. You’ll have a single room. Towels are included; bring your own toiletries.
Caller: What about meals? I don’t eat meat, and sometimes a residential course provides only a sandwich if you mention it too late.
Administrator: We can provide vegetarian meals. Please put vegetarian on the booking form rather than only telling the tutor, because the kitchen uses the form to plan. Breakfast is included in the room price. You can buy lunch and dinner here or use places in the village.
Caller: Do participants need to bring recording equipment? I have a laptop, but no special microphone.
Administrator: We’ll provide microphones and recorders. Bring headphones if you have a comfortable pair. We have some spares, but people often prefer their own for editing. Your laptop can be useful, though it’s not a requirement and we can supply a shared computer.
Caller: I may have a large bag because I’m continuing to visit family afterwards. Is there somewhere to leave it on Sunday after checkout?
Administrator: Yes, bags can stay in the office until the last session ends. They shouldn’t be left in the corridor, which is an emergency route. The workshop itself is on the ground floor, so you won’t need to carry the bag upstairs and down again.
Caller: Good. Is there preparation to complete before arriving?
Administrator: Please bring a photograph of a place you know. You’ll use it as a starting point for a short spoken piece. It needn’t be artistic, and it won’t be assessed as a photograph. We’re interested in the story it helps you tell, not the camera you used.
Caller: That sounds manageable. I’ll check the train now and complete the form tonight.
Administrator: I’ll send the travel sheet and provisional booking reference. Check the dates before paying, as there is a second radio course in the following month and the accommodation arrangements differ slightly.

listening.title: A guide to the town’s open-building weekend
listening.script:
Guide: Welcome to the information session for our open-building weekend. Several places normally closed to the public will offer visits, and the arrangements differ between sites. Please don’t assume that the ticket for one building lets you enter all the others. Most visits are free, but we still need to manage numbers and protect working spaces. I’ll explain five buildings first, then some general advice for planning your day. The leaflet contains addresses, and the updated website has the latest cancellation information.
The old courthouse is popular because people want to see the hearing room and the cells below. Only a limited number can enter each tour, so you must reserve a timed place before the weekend. We won’t maintain a queue for spare places at the door. If you can’t attend, cancel so someone else can use it. Booking several times in the hope of deciding later makes this much harder.
The clock workshop is reached by a steep staircase. There is no lift, and the narrow turn means we cannot install a temporary ramp. The ground-floor display remains available to everyone, but a visit to the workshop itself involves stairs. The leaflet states this clearly because we don’t want someone travelling across town only to discover the restriction on arrival.
At the recording studio, visitors can try making a short sound effect under supervision. Bring nothing special; the materials are supplied. The session is designed around participation rather than standing silently while someone describes equipment. Your recording can be sent to you afterwards if you choose to provide an address, but you don’t have to give one to take part.
The water tower offers the best view, but its opening depends on conditions. Strong wind makes the exposed upper platform unsuitable for visitors. Check the morning update before leaving home. We don’t cancel just because it’s cloudy, but safety takes priority over keeping a promise printed weeks earlier. A closure there doesn’t mean every other building will be closed.
The municipal greenhouse will stay open later than the other sites, until eight in the evening. That may help people who work during the day. Please use the marked paths because staff will still be maintaining plants in some sections. You can see those activities, but the site isn’t being converted into an unrestricted evening park.
---
For travel, we recommend the temporary circular bus. A ticket covers repeated journeys during the day, and the bus stops near all five sites. Walking between two nearby buildings is easy, but the whole circuit is longer than it appears on the small leaflet map. The service is intended to make combinations possible, not to require visitors to see every location in one day.
Please arrive for a reserved tour about ten minutes early. Earlier than that, there may be nowhere suitable to wait. A guide cannot delay the start for late arrivals because the next group needs its own full visit. If you miss a start, contact the booking desk rather than attempting to join through a side entrance.
Photography rules vary. You may photograph public displays where signs permit, but working documents on desks are not part of the exhibition. Ask before taking an identifiable photograph of an employee. Some are doing their ordinary jobs while visits take place, and being visible to the public isn’t agreement to appear in somebody’s online album.
Children are welcome on the family routes shown in the leaflet. Other tours include lengthy explanations or restricted spaces, so please read the age guidance. It isn’t a judgement about whether a particular child is well behaved. It’s information about what the organiser can provide safely and comfortably within that building.
At the end of a visit, you may be invited to suggest questions for next year’s programme. We particularly want to know what you’d like to understand about the work done inside these buildings. Requests simply to open more places are welcome, but a specific question helps us plan a useful visit rather than merely unlock another door. Staff have volunteered their time, and good questions make the exchange rewarding for them too.

listening.title: Preparing a student radio feature
listening.script:
Tutor: You’ve brought a draft plan for your radio feature. What’s the focus now?
Lena: We started with a general history of the night bus. It sounded too much like a list of dates, so we’re focusing on the people who use the last service and what the journey means in their routines.
Omar: We’d like to include different voices without pretending that three interviews represent everyone who travels at night.
Tutor: Good. What sound will help listeners understand the setting?
Lena: We recorded the bus arriving, but the engine overwhelms most of the conversation at the stop. We shouldn’t just turn up the voices because that also makes the background louder.
Omar: We could use a short arrival sound separately, then conduct the interviews a little way from the road. The sound can establish the scene without sitting under every spoken sentence.
Tutor: That would improve clarity. Remember that an atmospheric recording is useful only if it serves the story. You don’t need continuous noise to prove you were there.
Lena: We interviewed one passenger already. He gave a lovely account, but asked not to be identifiable. Could we keep the voice and omit the name?
Tutor: A distinctive voice or workplace detail may still identify him. Discuss the intended use with him and offer an alternative, such as reading an agreed extract with another speaker. Don’t assume that removing a name solves every privacy issue.
Omar: The transport office offered an official spokesperson. We should include that view, but perhaps not let it be the only explanation of why the timetable changed.
Tutor: Exactly. Ask which records support the explanation, and compare it with other evidence. Official status is relevant to the speaker’s role, not a guarantee that every interpretation is complete.
Lena: Our biggest editing problem is that all the interviews are interesting. We have enough for twenty minutes but the assignment allows eight.
Omar: We need to return to the central question and select material that advances it, even if a favourite anecdote has to go.
Tutor: That’s the discipline. Cutting should be guided by purpose, not by whether a sentence is easy to remove without changing your preferred argument.
---
Lena: We’ve divided the remaining work into five items. The opening sequence is drafted, but we want to play it to someone who hasn’t heard the story. If they can’t identify the setting and question, we should revise it.
Omar: The permission for the passenger extract is still unresolved. We’ll contact him again before using anything, not treat the earlier interview as blanket consent.
Tutor: Good. Put that ahead of polishing transitions. A beautifully edited extract you can’t use isn’t progress towards a finished feature.
Lena: The transport timetable is checked. We compared the current version with the archived one and confirmed the change date with the office, so that part is complete.
Omar: Our long music introduction is another matter. It takes almost a minute, which is too much in an eight-minute programme. We’ll remove it and retain only a brief transition where it helps listeners follow the change of scene.
Tutor: Ensure you have rights to whatever music remains. There is no need for a grand opening merely because professional programmes sometimes use one.
Lena: The final title is undecided. We have a working title, but we’ll choose the public one after the edit, when we know what the piece actually emphasises.
Omar: Otherwise we might force the material to fulfil a clever title we invented before listening properly. We’ll keep a few alternatives and ask what each one promises the audience.
Tutor: Sensible. When you deliver, include a short production note describing major editorial choices. Listeners won’t hear every decision, but the note should explain why you selected voices, separated sound from speech and omitted material. It makes the learning visible without turning the feature itself into a lecture about editing.

listening.title: Place names as historical evidence
listening.script:
Lecturer: A place name can remain familiar long after the feature it once described has disappeared. A street called Mill Lane may contain no mill, and a district named after a field may now be covered with houses. Today we’ll consider how names can contribute to historical enquiry and why they should not be treated as complete records by themselves. Our examples come from an invented district, so the purpose is to explain a method rather than make claims about a particular real community’s language or origins.
The first step is to collect forms of the name from different periods. Modern spelling may conceal earlier variations, and a single old map may contain an error. Researchers compare maps with deeds, directories and other dated documents. The sequence does not always show a neat progression from one form to another. Two spellings may coexist for many years. A record should preserve that variation instead of silently converting every historical form into the version printed on today’s sign, because the difference itself may be relevant evidence.
Pronunciation adds another source. Residents may say a name in a way that differs from what an outsider expects from its spelling. Interviews can preserve these spoken forms, though no individual speaker automatically represents an entire district. Age, neighbourhood and family history may all matter. With permission, researchers record speech and note the context of the interview. A recording without information about who was speaking and when can become difficult to interpret later, even when the sound quality is excellent.
Meaning is particularly tempting. A familiar modern word may appear inside a name, inviting an easy story about its origin. Yet the resemblance could be accidental, or the form could have changed from a different earlier word. Researchers need historical and linguistic evidence before accepting the attractive explanation. Local stories remain valuable as accounts of how residents understand a place, but that is not identical to demonstrating how the name first arose. The two questions can be studied together without pretending they have the same answer.
Maps also reveal spatial uncertainty. A name may move from a small feature to a larger area, or survive after a road is redirected. The modern boundary of a neighbourhood should not automatically be projected backwards onto every old reference. Researchers record what geographical extent a document appears to mean. Sometimes a description of adjoining properties is more useful than a bold label at the centre of a map. Names belong to practices of locating and describing places, not merely to fixed points waiting unchanged through time.
Official renaming creates another layer. A council decision may introduce a new name on signs while residents continue using the old one. Administrative records establish the formal change date, but everyday adoption can be gradual and uneven. Delivery workers, schools and local newspapers may use different forms. Studying that transition requires several kinds of evidence. A decree tells us what was authorised, not exactly what everyone said the following morning. Treating official documents as a complete account of usage would miss a large part of the social history.
The project must also consider consent and sensitivity. Some names carry associations that residents find painful, while others are closely connected with a minority community’s identity. Publishing an origin story can affect present debates, even when the researcher thinks of the work as purely historical. This is not a reason to suppress evidence, but it is a reason to explain uncertainty and consult people who may be affected. A neat public label should not turn a disputed interpretation into an apparently settled fact just because a display has limited space.
Finally, a useful catalogue links each claim to its source. It separates an attested form from a proposed meaning and records alternatives where the evidence remains inconclusive. The aim is not to make every name mysterious. Some have clear and well-supported histories. It is to prevent the ease of repeating a story from being mistaken for the strength of its evidence. Names can connect everyday journeys to a deeper history when researchers preserve the route by which they reached their conclusions, including the points where that route still divides.

paragraphs.A: The fictional district of Wendon contained a modern central library and several villages whose residents rarely visited it. Bus services were infrequent, and opening hours overlapped with many people's working day. The district's first response was to advertise its online collection more widely. That helped some readers but assumed access to reliable connections and suitable devices. Librarian Noor Hale proposed a different experiment: small staffed collection points in places people already used. The aim was not to reproduce a full library in every village, but to reduce the effort needed to obtain particular services.
paragraphs.B: A room beside a food shop became the first collection point. Residents could request books from the central catalogue and collect them during two weekly sessions. Hale rejected the suggestion that requests should be made exclusively online. A telephone line and paper slips allowed people to use the service without learning a new interface. Staff entered those requests into the same system, so stock records remained consistent. This extra work was counted in the project budget rather than treated as free labour that would somehow be absorbed by existing staff alongside all their other duties.
paragraphs.C: Choosing a venue involved compromises. A village hall had more space, but stood on the outskirts and opened mainly for planned events. The food shop offered less room but attracted regular visits. The library paid a modest rent for the adjoining room and installed a lockable cabinet for requested items. Books were not left on open shelves overnight. A small selection was available for browsing during staffed sessions, yet most of the stock remained at the central building. This preserved the benefit of a shared collection rather than dividing it into tiny permanent holdings.
paragraphs.D: Transport initially followed a fixed route on one morning each week. A missed request could therefore produce a long wait. The team added a late request deadline for urgent educational materials and arranged space in a council vehicle already travelling between offices. This did not create an on-demand courier service, but reduced some avoidable delays without requiring a dedicated journey. The timetable was printed beside request forms. Residents could see when an item was likely to arrive instead of receiving an optimistic promise that staff could not reliably keep.
paragraphs.E: The collection point also attracted questions unrelated to borrowing. People asked for help understanding forms, finding local history photographs and using audio books on a phone. Hale trained staff to recognise when they could help and when a specialist referral was needed. The library did not collect copies of private financial documents or complete applications on residents' behalf. A quiet screen allowed conversations to be less audible to other visitors. These boundaries protected both users and staff while acknowledging that access to information often begins with a question more complicated than a book title.
paragraphs.F: After six months, the district compared borrowing records with a short household survey. Borrowing had increased, but the survey showed that some residents still did not understand which services were available. Others knew about the point but could not attend either weekly session. One opening was moved to an evening after consultation with shop staff. The evaluation also distinguished new users from existing library members who had simply switched collection location. Both groups benefited, but confusing them would exaggerate how many previously excluded people the experiment had reached.
paragraphs.G: Expansion brought a new concern: volunteers offered to run additional points without paid staff. Their enthusiasm was welcome, yet Hale argued that a reliable public service could not depend entirely on whoever happened to be free. Volunteers helped with publicity and reading events, while trained employees retained responsibility for records, privacy and referrals. The district expanded to three more venues, with a published rota and cover for absence. Growth was slower than a volunteer-only model might have allowed, but opening times became a commitment residents could plan around rather than an informal possibility.
paragraphs.H: Wendon's experiment did not make the central library redundant. Its collection, professional expertise and specialist spaces supported the smaller points. Nor could a collection cabinet provide everything that a welcoming building offered. The district described the service as a network with different functions rather than a contest between physical and digital access. Its achievement lay in connecting shared resources to ordinary journeys and offering several ways to ask for help. The lesson was not that libraries require fewer people, but that their people and materials can be organised around the obstacles that prevent use.

reading.title: Watching change one picture at a time

paragraphs.A: Pictures contributed by the public can form a record of environmental change, but an attractive collection of images is not automatically a comparable dataset. A photograph of a tree may show its leaves clearly while revealing little about the date, location or conditions of observation. In a fictional project called Seasonal Streets, researchers invited residents to photograph selected trees throughout the year. The project sought to understand local differences in seasonal events, not to identify the single earliest leaf in the country. Its success depended on ordinary observations being repeated in sufficiently consistent ways.
paragraphs.B: Project scientist Lina Moss designed a simple protocol. Participants chose a marked viewing position and included the same branch in each picture. They also recorded the date and whether buds, open leaves or fallen leaves were visible. Moss knew that these categories compressed a continuous process into discrete labels. She supplied examples of borderline stages and allowed an uncertain category. Requiring a definite answer for every image would create apparent precision by hiding genuine disagreement. The project preferred a visible gap in certainty to a confident classification that the photograph could not support.
paragraphs.C: Photographer Evan Cole worried that participants would move to obtain a more appealing composition. He demonstrated why a less beautiful but consistent viewpoint was often more useful. If one week showed a sunny outer branch and the next showed the shaded centre of the tree, an apparent change could reflect framing rather than development. Cole made a short guide using deliberately ordinary photographs. The purpose was not to train residents as professional photographers. It was to show which visual decisions affected the comparison and which, such as including an untidy fence in the background, usually did not matter.
paragraphs.D: Analyst Priya Nair examined missing observations. Trees near busy routes attracted more photographs, while those at the end of quiet streets were often neglected. A period of bad weather produced fewer submissions even though seasonal change continued. Nair warned against interpreting the average of submitted pictures as if the same places had been observed on every date. She tracked each tree separately and reported the number of observations behind each summary. Participants could then see why a smooth town-wide curve might conceal irregular evidence and why more photographs did not necessarily mean a more representative sample.
paragraphs.E: Community organiser Hugo Reyes concentrated on who could participate. A phone-based submission tool was convenient, but some residents preferred a camera and a paper record. The project offered monthly drop-in sessions where staff uploaded those images with the contributor. Reyes also arranged pairs so that a participant away from home could ask another person to photograph the same branch. These arrangements made continuity a shared responsibility. They did not eliminate all barriers, but they avoided treating ownership of a recent smartphone and constant personal availability as necessary qualifications for noticing a local tree.
paragraphs.F: The first year's results showed earlier leaf development on several sheltered streets. The team resisted attributing the entire difference to temperature because tree species, age and management also varied. A second phase added paired observations of the same species in contrasting locations. It also recorded pruning, which could remove the photographed branch or change the exposure of the remaining leaves. These additions emerged from uncertainty in the first phase rather than from an attempt to make the initial findings sound more decisive. An exploratory project can be useful by revealing what a later comparison needs to control.
paragraphs.G: Participants reported benefits that were not part of the scientific measurement. Some began noticing insects or discussing the street's history with neighbours. The team welcomed these outcomes but kept them separate from claims about the quality of the seasonal data. A socially valuable activity can still generate uneven evidence, and a rigorous measurement can still be unwelcoming to many residents. Evaluating both purposes required more than a single participation total. The organisers asked what people learned, which observations were usable and whose experience remained absent, without expecting one measure to answer all three questions.
paragraphs.H: Seasonal Streets illustrates a productive relationship between public participation and technical care. Standardisation did not require eliminating every personal contribution; it identified the details that had to remain stable for a particular question. Flexibility elsewhere made participation possible. The photographs became evidence through context, repetition and honest reporting of omissions. Their greatest strength was not that many people could collect pictures cheaply. It was that repeated local attention could connect an abstract question about change with a visible object in everyday life, while leaving enough information for someone else to assess the resulting claim.

paragraphs.A: Convenience is usually presented as an obvious benefit: a task takes less time, demands fewer steps or can be completed from home. These improvements can matter greatly, particularly to someone with limited mobility or inflexible working hours. Yet a service can become more convenient for its typical user while becoming harder for others to use. A change may also move effort from a paid worker to the customer without making that effort disappear. To evaluate convenience seriously, we need to ask whose effort is counted, when it occurs and which alternatives remain available.
paragraphs.B: Consider a fictional sports centre that replaces its staffed booking desk with an application. Regular players can reserve a court in seconds, even when the building is closed. For them, the change is a clear improvement. A visitor with an older phone, an unfamiliar payment card or limited reading ability may face several failed attempts before receiving help. Counting the average booking time among successful app users excludes these attempts by definition. The resulting figure can be accurate as a description of one group and misleading as a description of the service as a whole.
paragraphs.C: This is not a reason to preserve every inconvenient process. Staffed desks also impose costs: journeys, queues and restricted hours. The stronger conclusion is that comparisons need a complete account of the work involved. A user who spends twenty minutes setting up an account may recover that time over many later bookings, while an occasional visitor may never do so. Initial effort and repeated effort should therefore be distinguished. The same design can be highly convenient for frequent use and poorly suited to a task someone needs only once a year.
paragraphs.D: Automation can also remove small conversations that previously performed an unrecognised function. A receptionist might notice that a new player has booked an unsuitable court or explain a cancellation rule before payment. An application can provide equivalent guidance, but only if the designers know the conversation mattered. Replacing a desk with a form while copying only its visible transaction may omit the informal checking around it. What looked like wasted time may have prevented later mistakes. The task is to identify useful interactions, not to assume that every human exchange is either essential or inefficient.
paragraphs.E: There is a further issue of control. A convenient subscription renewal can prevent an interruption, but a difficult cancellation can turn convenience into one-sided dependence. Friction is the effort a process imposes. Removing it from joining while retaining it in leaving serves the provider more clearly than the customer. Some friction is legitimate, such as confirming a decision with serious consequences. Its justification should depend on the decision's risk rather than on whether the provider benefits from delay. A service that makes actions easy only when profitable offers a selective kind of convenience.
paragraphs.F: Support routes matter especially when a standard process fails. A beautifully designed form cannot anticipate every circumstance, and repeating the same instructions is not useful when the instructions assume something false about the user. An effective exception route allows a person to describe the problem to someone with authority to resolve it. This route may be used rarely and still be essential. Its value should not be judged solely by the proportion of routine transactions it handles, just as an emergency exit is not evaluated by how often people choose it for ordinary entry.
paragraphs.G: Organisations often reply that maintaining alternatives is expensive. Sometimes that is true, and resources are finite. But the cost comparison should include work displaced onto users and the later costs of unresolved errors. Offering a telephone route for occasional exceptions may be cheaper than rebuilding every digital screen, while clearer instructions may reduce calls. There is no universal requirement to operate every possible channel forever. There is a requirement to examine the consequences of removing a channel instead of treating the savings on one departmental budget as the whole social result.
paragraphs.H: Convenience is best understood as a relationship between a service and a situation, not a permanent property of an interface. A well-designed system can make routine tasks quick, preserve reasonable alternatives and handle unusual cases without humiliation or excessive delay. It should be evaluated with unsuccessful attempts visible, not only completed transactions. The aim is not to celebrate difficulty or resist technology. It is to make the promise of reduced effort honest: an improvement should not be declared complete merely because the people still struggling have disappeared from the measurement.

writing.prompt: The plans show the layout of Market Square in the fictional town of Elwick in 2005 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
writing.visual:
![Market Square plans](writing-1.svg)

The plans use the same boundaries and orientation (north at the top). Main Road remains along the south edge.

| Position inside square | 2005 | 2025 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Northwest | Car park | Community garden |
| Northeast | Shops | Shops, same footprint |
| Centre | Road connecting west and east entrances | Pedestrian path connecting west and east entrances |
| Southwest | Bus stop | Café with outdoor seating |
| Southeast | Public toilets | Public toilets, same footprint |
| North-central | No structure | Covered market pavilion |

In 2025 the bus stop is on Main Road outside the square, immediately south of its former position. Vehicle entrances at the east and west have become pedestrian entrances. No scale or building dimensions are supplied.
writing.guidance: Overview: the square becomes pedestrian-oriented, with greenery and a pavilion. The car park becomes a garden; the internal bus stop becomes café/seating, with the bus stop moved onto Main Road. Shops and toilets remain; the east–west road becomes a pedestrian path. Avoid claiming all transport is removed from the surrounding area or inferring relative building sizes from an unscaled plan.

writing.guidance: Develop the value of intergenerational contact and of age-specific needs or interests. A combined approach can be argued, with examples of which activities suit each arrangement.
